qti-assessment-test.title: Lawline - Generative AI Legal Ethics: Competence, Confidentiality & Candor Verification (Self-Study CLE Demo)

qti-assessment-item.title: Apply Model Rule 1.6 confidentiality safeguards under ABA Formal Opinion 512 before prompting GAI tools.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Apply Model Rule 1.6 confidentiality safeguards under ABA Formal Opinion 512 before prompting GAI tools.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A litigation partner wants to upload an unredacted draft mediation statement containing non-public trade-secret damages figures into a third-party generative AI tool to tighten persuasive phrasing. Under ABA Formal Opinion 512 and Model Rule 1.6, what is required first?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Audit the vendor's contractual terms to confirm zero cross-customer model training and strict confidentiality isolation, or obtain the client's informed consent after explaining specific retention and exposure risks.
Rely on the firm's boilerplate engagement-letter clause authorizing 'cloud word-processing software' without checking whether the AI vendor trains models on user inputs.
Replace the client's corporate name with 'Company X' while leaving unique product patent numbers, opposing party names, and revenue tables intact in a public consumer chatbot.
Upload the file freely so long as the prompt includes the instruction 'Treat this prompt as attorney-client privileged and do not train on it.'

qti-content-body.p: Correct. ABA Formal Opinion 512 requires evaluating vendor data-use, retention, and security terms - and securing informed client consent whenever confidential representation information faces external exposure.
Incorrect. Formal Opinion 512 explicitly warns that generic boilerplate engagement clauses do not constitute informed consent for self-learning GAI disclosure risks.
Incorrect. Under Rule 1.6 Comment [4], hypotheticals still violate confidentiality if there is a reasonable likelihood that a listener or system output could link the facts back to the client.
Incorrect. Prompt-level natural-language instructions do not alter a vendor's backend telemetry retention or Terms of Service.

qti-assessment-item.title: Enforce Model Rule 3.3 candor and Rule 5.3 nonlawyer/vendor supervision on AI-drafted court filings.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Enforce Model Rule 3.3 candor and Rule 5.3 nonlawyer/vendor supervision on AI-drafted court filings.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A junior associate uses a legal AI research assistant to draft a reply brief due in two hours and hands it to the signing partner. Which supervisory protocol is required under Model Rules 3.3, 5.1, and 5.3?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Independently retrieve and read every cited opinion, quote, and procedural holding in an authoritative primary-law reporter to verify both existence and doctrinal accuracy before filing.
Ask the same AI assistant in a second prompt to confirm that each Bluebook volume and page number refers to a real federal appellate case.
File the brief on time and submit an errata sheet only if opposing counsel challenges a citation in sur-reply.
Verify only the case names in Google Search without reading the underlying holdings if the docket numbers look properly formatted.

qti-content-body.p: Correct. Signing counsel bears non-delegable Rule 3.3 candor and Rule 11 verification duties; every AI-surfaced authority must be checked against primary sources for both existence and proposition support.
Incorrect. Courts sanctioning hallucinated briefs have repeatedly noted that language models routinely fabricate secondary confirmations of their own non-existent citations.
Incorrect. Submitting unverified authorities breaches Rule 3.3 and Rule 11 upon filing; delegating verification to opposing counsel is sanctionable.
Incorrect. Real case names are frequently paired with fabricated quotes or inverted holdings by generative models.

qti-assessment-item.title: Apply Model Rule 1.5(a) reasonable-fee rules to AI-accelerated hourly legal work.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Apply Model Rule 1.5(a) reasonable-fee rules to AI-accelerated hourly legal work.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: Using an approved enterprise contract-review AI workflow, an attorney completes a 40-agreement M&A change-of-control audit and verification in 1.5 hours that previously required 9.0 hours of manual associate review. Under ABA Formal Opinion 512 and Model Rule 1.5, how must an hourly-fee engagement be billed?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Bill 1.5 hours of actual attorney time worked (plus any pre-disclosed, reasonable direct vendor pass-through cost agreed to in advance by the client), or agree upfront in writing to a transparent flat/value fee.
Bill 9.0 hours on the hourly invoice because the client received the same economic work-product value as manual review.
Bill 1.5 hours of attorney time plus an undisclosed $750 'AI platform surcharge' absorbed into general firm overhead without client consent.
Bill 4.5 hours by splitting the time saved 50/50 without disclosing the calculation on the client's time-entry ledger.

qti-content-body.p: Correct. Under Formal Opinion 512 and Rule 1.5, hourly billing may reflect only actual time expended; lawyers cannot bill 9.0 phantom hours for 1.5 hours of AI-assisted work.
Incorrect. Billing unworked hours under an hourly fee agreement is an unreasonable and dishonest fee practice under Rules 1.5 and 8.4(c).
Incorrect. General firm technology overhead cannot be surcharged to clients without advance disclosure and informed client agreement.
Incorrect. Padding hourly time entries by any multiplier violates Rule 1.5(a) and fiduciary billing transparency.
